Turbid describes something — most commonly a liquid — that is cloudy, murky, and unclear because it has tiny particles floating and suspended through it. You cannot see through it clearly. It is the opposite of clear, clean, or transparent.

Think of a glass of clean drinking water. It is perfectly clear — light passes straight through it and you can see to the bottom without any difficulty. Now imagine stirring a handful of soil into that same glass. The water immediately turns brown and murky. You can no longer see through it. That water is turbid.

The cloudiness in turbid things is caused by suspended particles — tiny bits of matter that are floating throughout the liquid without fully dissolving into it. These particles could be:

  • Silt, mud, or clay (in rivers and floodwater)
  • Sand or fine soil (in disturbed lakes or ponds)
  • Algae and microscopic organisms (in stagnant water)
  • Sediment stirred up from the bottom of a water body
  • Ash or smoke particles (in air, less commonly)

The key idea is that these particles are not dissolved — they are just floating around, scattering light and blocking your view. This is what makes turbid different from simply "colored" water. Turbid water looks thick, heavy, and unclear.

• A river after heavy rainfall becomes turbid because rainwater washes soil and silt into it from the surrounding land. This is probably the single most classic use of the word.
  • Floodwater is almost always turbid — it looks dark brown or tan because it has picked up enormous amounts of debris and sediment as it flows.
  • A pond that has been disturbed — say, by a person wading through it — becomes turbid as the sediment at the bottom gets kicked up into the water.
  • Ocean water near a beach after a storm can turn turbid as waves churn up sand from the sea floor.
  • A glass of water with stirred mud is about as turbid as things get in everyday life.

There is a subtle but important distinction here. Cloudy is a general word — you can say a glass is cloudy, the sky is cloudy, or someone's vision is cloudy. Turbid, however, almost always carries the specific implication that the cloudiness comes from suspended matter in a fluid. It is a more precise and technical word. Scientists, ecologists, and environmental workers use it frequently when measuring water quality, because how turbid a body of water is tells you a lot about pollution levels, soil erosion, and aquatic health.

So while all turbid water is cloudy, not all cloudy things are turbid — turbid has that specific sense of being made unclear by particles floating within a substance.

Beyond the physical, literal world, turbid is also used figuratively to describe thinking, writing, speech, or ideas that are confused, muddled, and hard to follow — just as turbid water is hard to see through, turbid thought is hard to think through clearly.

If a philosopher's argument is turbid, it means their reasoning is tangled, obscure, and difficult to understand — not necessarily because the topic is hard, but because the thinking itself is muddled. If a writer's prose is turbid, it means their sentences are convoluted, overloaded, and unclear.

This figurative use follows naturally from the literal one: just as muddy particles cloud water and prevent you from seeing through it, confused ideas cloud a mind or a piece of writing and prevent you from understanding it.

Examples of figurative use:

  • "His turbid thinking led him to contradict himself three times in a single paragraph."
  • "The turbid prose of the report made a simple idea nearly impossible to grasp."
How Strong a Word Is It?

Turbid is not a mild word. It does not mean slightly hazy or a little unclear. It implies a notable, significant degree of cloudiness or confusion — enough that it is genuinely difficult to see through or understand. If water is described as turbid, you should picture it looking heavily discolored and murky, not just a tiny bit off.
How Turbid Compares to Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but each has its own flavor:

Murky is the word most people reach for in everyday speech instead of turbid. Murky means dark and gloomy in an unclear way, and it often carries a slightly threatening or mysterious tone — "murky waters," "murky motives." Turbid is more clinical and precise, and more specifically tied to particle-caused cloudiness. In everyday writing you can use them interchangeably, but in scientific or formal writing, turbid is the more accurate choice.

Muddy is the informal, everyday cousin. Muddy water and turbid water are often the same thing, but turbid sounds educated and precise while muddy sounds casual and straightforward.

Opaque means you cannot see through something at all — zero transparency. Turbid water may be very dark but it does not always mean completely opaque. Turbid describes a spectrum of cloudiness rather than total blockage.

Hazy is typically used for air, mist, or distance — a hazy sky, a hazy memory. Turbid is rarely used for air and is not the right word for a hazy memory; that would be figuratively murky or unclear.

Since you will almost certainly encounter it, the noun form of turbid is turbidity — it refers to the degree or quality of being turbid. Scientists measure turbidity in water using special instruments, and it is a standard way to assess water quality. High turbidity means very cloudy water; low turbidity means clear water. Knowing this will help you recognize the word in scientific or environmental contexts.

Turbid (adjective): Cloudy, murky, and unclear — describing a liquid (or sometimes a gas) in which tiny particles are suspended, making it impossible to see through cleanly. By extension, also used to describe thinking, writing, or ideas that are muddled and hard to understand. It is a formal, precise word, stronger than "slightly cloudy," and most at home describing rivers, floodwater, or polluted water — and in figurative use, confused or convoluted thought.
